planting.note: Start from rooted stem cuttings or divisions of the spreading rhizomes in spring; pot into a light, fast-draining mix and keep in bright, indirect light through the growing season. Grown as a houseplant in most climates; only reliably hardy outdoors in frost-free zones.

directions: This is the true botanical Gloxinia genus, distinct from the florist's Sinningia speciosa that borrows its name in the trade. Pot in a loose, humus-rich mix that drains quickly, and place where it gets bright indirect light through an east or filtered south window; leggy, sparse-flowering growth signals too little light. Clusters of nodding, orange-red tubular flowers with yellow throats appear at the stem tips in cooler months, held above soft, hairy, scalloped leaves on an upright, slightly woody stem. Water when the top inch of soil dries, reduce watering in winter rest, and pinch young growth to keep the naturally lanky habit full and well branched.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — Gloxinia sylvatica
Smithsonian Gardens — Gesneriad collection notes on Gloxinia vs. Sinningia
North Carolina State University Extension — Gesneriaceae houseplants

planting.note: Root 3–4 inch stem tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light mix, then transplant into a hanging basket once rooted. Best started in spring or early summer so plants establish before winter's lower light. Grown year-round as a houseplant.

directions: An epiphytic trailing gesneriad best grown in a hanging basket filled with a chunky, fast-draining mix of peat, perlite, and orchid bark, mimicking its native life on tree branches in Central and South American rainforests. Give it bright, indirect light — an east window or a few feet back from a south window — and let the mix dry slightly between waterings, since the fleshy leaves store some moisture and resent constant sogginess. Small white to pale pink tubular flowers appear singly along the trailing stems nearly year-round, followed by round orange-red berries that persist for weeks and give the plant its common name. Regular light misting or a nearby humidity tray helps replicate the moist air of its native habitat and keeps the small, glossy leaves from crisping at the edges.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — Codonanthe care sheet
Missouri Botanical Garden — Gesneriaceae houseplant culture
Selby Botanical Gardens — Epiphytic gesneriads of the American tropics

planting.note: Start dormant tubers in shallow trays of barely moist mix in late winter to early spring, tuber crown just at the soil surface. Sold and grown as a potted houseplant; goes dormant and can be stored dry over winter like other tuberous sinningias.

directions: A tuberous, shrubby gesneriad grown for its clusters of brilliant red-orange tubular flowers held above velvety, silver-haired foliage, formerly classified in the genus Rechsteineria. Give it bright indirect light — a lightly shaded east or south window works well — and pot in a loose, well-drained mix, since the tuber rots quickly in wet, heavy soil. Water thoroughly and let the top of the mix dry before watering again, and stop watering once foliage yellows in fall so the tuber can rest dry and cool through winter. Its hairy leaves and stems make it prone to water-spotting, so water at the soil line rather than overhead and keep it away from cold drafts.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — Sinningia cardinalis (formerly Rechsteineria cardinalis)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Gesneriads for indoor flowering
Gesneriad Reference Web (Gesneriad Society) — Sinningia species culture

planting.note: Root 4–6 inch stem tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat-based mix, then move to a hanging basket once new growth shows. Best propagated in spring or summer for full establishment before winter. Grown indoors year-round outside frost-free tropical climates.

directions: Grown chiefly for its foliage rather than its modest greenish-yellow flowers, this trailing epiphyte carries thick, glossy leaves patterned with silvery-green marbling on top and maroon-purple undersides, a striking contrast that intensifies in bright, indirect light. Pot in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix of bark, perlite, and peat, and let the mix dry slightly between waterings — like its lipstick-plant relatives it dislikes soggy roots but wants regular humidity around the foliage. Best displayed in a hanging basket where the 2–3 foot trailing stems can cascade and show off the leaf undersides. Feed lightly during active spring and summer growth and keep away from cold drafts, which cause leaf drop.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — Aeschynanthus species culture
Missouri Botanical Garden — Aeschynanthus care
Gesneriad Reference Web — Aeschynanthus marmoratus

planting.note: Root 4–6 inch stem cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat mix, then pot into a hanging basket once rooted. Best rooted in spring or early summer so trailing stems fill out before shorter winter days. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.

directions: A finer-textured, more densely trailing relative of the larger Columnea gloriosa, this epiphyte carries tiny rounded leaves along thin, wiry stems that can cascade 2–3 feet from a hanging basket. Pot in a loose, fast-draining epiphytic mix and grow in bright, indirect light — direct sun scorches the small leaves, while too little light suppresses the tubular red-orange flowers that appear along the stems in winter and early spring. Keep humidity moderate to high and let the mix dry slightly between waterings, since the fine roots are prone to rot in constantly wet mix. A cooler winter rest period with reduced watering encourages the heaviest bloom the following season.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — Columnea species culture
Gesneriad Reference Web — Columnea microphylla
North Carolina State University Extension — Gesneriaceae houseplants

planting.note: Propagate by rooting the plantlets that form on trailing stolons, or by division of an established mat; pot into shallow, wide containers or hanging baskets. Best started in spring or summer. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.

directions: Unlike its bolder, colorful-leaved cousin Episcia cupreata, this species is grown for its abundant small white flowers with deeply fringed, lace-like edges, set against small, plain green, quilted leaves on wiry trailing stolons. Grow in bright, indirect to shaded light — an east window or a spot a few feet from a south window — since direct sun stresses the thin foliage. Pot in a light, peaty, well-drained mix and keep evenly moist without letting the pot sit in water; consistently high humidity encourages the heaviest, most continuous bloom. Excellent in a hanging basket or as a groundcover in a large terrarium, where the trailing stems root into the mix as they spread and can be divided freely to share or restart plants.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — Episcia dianthiflora
Gesneriad Reference Web — Episcia species culture

common_name: Blue Trailing Achimenes (Long-Flowered Hot Water Plant)

planting.note: Start dormant scaly rhizomes shallowly in moist, warm potting mix in early to mid spring; growth is slow to emerge and stalls in cool soil below roughly 70°F, hence the 'hot water plant' nickname referring to the warm water once traditionally used to break dormancy. Grown as a warm-season houseplant or basket plant, dormant and dry over winter.

directions: The classic wild species behind many modern Achimenes hybrids, valued for its abundant violet-blue, flared, tubular flowers held just above soft, slightly hairy, toothed leaves on lax, semi-trailing stems. Grow in bright, indirect light with some protection from hot midday sun, and pot in a light, humus-rich mix that stays evenly moist through the growing season without becoming waterlogged. High humidity keeps the foliage lush; dry air can cause leaf edges to brown. As the flowering season winds down in fall, gradually withhold water and let the top growth die back, then store the small scaly rhizomes dry and cool until repotting the following spring.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — Achimenes species culture
Gesneriad Reference Web — Achimenes longiflora
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Gesneriads for indoor flowering

planting.note: Root 3–4 inch stem tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light mix, then transplant into a hanging basket once rooted. Best started in spring or summer so trailing stems fill in before lower-light winter months. Grown indoors year-round as a houseplant.

directions: A widely sold cultivar distinguished from the plain-flowered Nematanthus gregarius by its boldly striped, pouch-shaped flowers — glossy orange-red tipped with bright yellow, resembling a piece of candy corn nestled among small, thick, glossy leaves on trailing stems. Grow in bright, indirect light for the heaviest bloom; low light produces lush foliage but few flowers. Pot in a light, fast-draining mix and let the top inch dry between waterings, since the succulent-like leaves store some moisture and the roots resent constant wet. Best displayed in a hanging basket where the 2 foot trailing stems can cascade freely, and pinch stem tips after flushes of bloom to keep growth dense.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — Nematanthus cultivars
Gesneriad Reference Web — Nematanthus 'Tropicana'

planting.note: Propagate by dividing offsets that form around the base of the rosette, or by rooting individual leaves in moist mix as with African violets. Grown indoors year-round as a compact houseplant or terrarium plant.

directions: A rosette-forming gesneriad from southern China grown much like an African violet, with thick, quilted leaves marked by a silvery sheen along the veins and clusters of small, pale yellow tubular flowers rising just above the foliage. Grow in bright, indirect light or under fluorescent or LED plant lights, since direct sun bleaches the patterned leaves. Pot in a light, fast-draining mix in a shallow container that matches the rosette's modest root system, and water from the base or around the crown to avoid rot at the center of the rosette. Its compact size makes it well suited to a windowsill collection or a covered terrarium, where the extra humidity keeps the leaf margins from browning.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — Chirita and Primulina species culture
Gesneriad Reference Web — Chirita sinensis
